newsitem.title: UK: Full text of June UK PMI services survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of June UK PMI services survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the PMI services survey conducted by the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS), sponsored by Reuters.
The CIPS survey of the UK service economy shows growth of business activity remained strong in June, generating employment but also further price pressures.

The seasonally adjusted Business Activity Index registered 62.9 in June, down slightly on the May figure but still the third highest reading since this survey began a year ago. One in three service companies reported business activity to have risen in June while only 8.0% reported a decline. Growth was generally attributable to increased confidence in the economy and the resurgence of the "feel-good factor", especially amongst consumers.

Companies further boosted employment to expand capacity and meet strong growth of new business. One in five companies recruited new staff -- twice as many as saw staff levels fall. However, the latest increase in employment was again insufficient to fully boost capacity to meet the strong growth of new business. The level of business outstanding at panel member companies (that is, work in hand but not yet completed) rose again in June as a result.

The inability to raise capacity in part reflected the persistence of skill shortages. The June survey saw a deceleration in the rate of growth of employment largely due to companies having difficulties finding suitably qualified staff to replace leavers. In other cases, higher wages or salaries were again having to be offered to either attract new staff or retain existing staff.
The resulting rise in labour costs was reflected in a further rise in average input prices in June, although the rate of inflation moderated for the second month running.

With input costs rising and demand for services continuing to strengthen, service companies were again able to raise charges and thereby pass higher costs -- at least in part -- onto customers. This contrasts sharply with the situation last year, when this survey found charges to have been falling as firms competed for business. However, the incidence of firms successfully raising charges remains relatively low: whereas 15 percent of companies reported a rise in input prices only 10 percent were able to raise charges for their services.
Optimism concerning activity remained steady with three quarters of all companies surveyed expecting business to pick up further over the next twelve months. Only 5 percent expect a deterioration.
INCOMING NEW BUSINESS

The amount of new business placed at panel member companies continued to show strong growth in June, although the seasonally adjusted pace of growth weakened to the slowest rate seen since January. Nevertheless, a third of all companies saw an increase in new business during the month, three times as many as reported a decline. The most commonly reported factor to have driven the rise in demand for services was greater consumer confidence with an associated rise in housing market activity. OUTSTANDING BUSINESS

The seasonally adjusted Outstanding Business Index dipped slightly in June but remained well above 50.0 and thereby signalled a further rise in the amount of work in hand but yet to be completed at panel member companies. The rate at which new business has grown recently has frequently exceeded the rate at which panel members have been able to expand capacity in the short term. Certain skill shortages were again cited as a constraint on expansion by some companies.
EMPLOYMENT

Service sector employment rose significantly again in June as one in five companies recruited additional staff to expand capacity and meet growth of new business. The pace of employment growth slowed slightly, but this reflected an increased incidence of staff leaving voluntarily -- and an inability of firms to find suitable replacements -- rather than a rise in the number of companies announcing redundancies. Employment has shown significant growth in each month since this survey began.
PRICES CHARGED

Average prices charged by service providers rose for the eighth consecutive month in June and at a rate of growth only slightly down on that recorded in the previous month. In contrast to last year, when this survey found charges to have been falling, the continued strengthening of demand has allowed companies to pass higher costs onto customers in recent months. However, the rate of increase signalled by the survey remained moderate with only one in ten companies successfully raising their charges in June.
INPUT PRICES

Rising wages and salaries were again the driving force behind a further increase in average input prices in June, with higher interest rates providing an additional source of cost pressure. Companies within all main sectors of the service economy continued to report that significant salary increases were often having to be offered in order to retain existing staff or to attract suitably qualified new employees. The index declined for the second month running, however, suggesting a modest easing in the rate of input price inflation.
BUSINESS EXPECTATIONS

Business optimism in the service sector remained relatively stable in June. Only 5.0 percent of firms expected sales to be significantly subdued by either rising taxes, interest rates or the strength of sterling over the next year while around three quarters of the panel expected levels of business activity to rise. The buoyancy of business confidence was again spread evenly across all main sectors of the service economy with increased sales and marketing activity generally expected to provide the main source of new business.
-- Rosemary Bennett, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
